facts.claim: The song was co-written by Jacob Collier and Lizzy McAlpine. McAlpine sings on it and John Mayer plays guitar.
Collier says he wrote the song in the depths of lockdown the year before its release, with his friend Lizzy McAlpine.

Collier says he wanted to explore the emotional world of isolation, loss and memory. He did this by piecing together a tapestry of soft orchestral sounds, blurring the lines between reality and imagination.
Collier told Rolling Stone that having John Mayer lend his guitar tones was a surreal thrill. He said he grew up listening to Mayer's music in a deep way.
Collier and McAlpine trade verses and their voices intermingle on the chorus, over Mayer's guitar.
It was released on 10 June 2022 as Collier's first official single since Djesse Vol. 3. That album earned three nominations at the 2021 Grammys, including Album of the Year.
The song later appeared on Djesse Vol. 4 (released 29 February 2024), the fourth and final instalment of the Djesse series. Collier produced all of that album's tracks except "Wherever I Go".
On Djesse Vol. 4, the song credits Collier, McAlpine and Mayer as writers. It contains a sample of Collier's "In Too Deep (Acoustic Version)".
Discogs credits John Mayer with the electric guitar solo on the Djesse Vol. 4 version of the song. Emily Lazar is credited as mastering engineer for the album.

The trio first performed the song live together at Lizzy McAlpine's 6 October 2022 show at the Troubadour in Los Angeles. McAlpine and Collier played acoustic guitars and Mayer played a Charvel Custom Shop San Dimas.

research.lineage: The song sits in the lineage of Collier's genre-blending, harmony-heavy pop and R&B, a style that grew out of his YouTube multi-instrumental, layered-vocal arrangements and runs through the Djesse series.

draft:
A patch of sunlight on a carpet is a small thing to build a song around, and that smallness is the point. **Never Gonna Be Alone** opens with the narrator looking at the spot "on the carpet where I held you for a moment in June," and everything after is an effort to stay inside that moment. Jacob Collier wrote it with his friend Lizzy McAlpine in the depths of lockdown, and he has said he wanted to explore isolation, loss and memory. You can hear all three in where the lyric goes: a room, a window, a door, a garden at night with a tree looking up at the moon. Nobody leaves home. The person being loved exists only as a place.

The chorus is where the feeling splits. "You'll be right where I left you, sitting on the floor" sounds like comfort, a lover waiting and unchanged. But only a memory can stay that still. So when the line turns to the title, the promise of never being alone is also an admission that the real company is gone. The bridge says so outright, "Even though I know / Nothing's gonna change," then swerves straight back to devotion, vowing to keep finding the way back. The song never settles whether that return is healing or a trap. It holds gratitude and grief in the same hand.

The sound matches that hush. Fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through arpeggios, a bass walks underneath, and brushed drums keep a slow, relaxed sway. The room is spacious, the reverb soft, the whole thing warm and polished. Collier and McAlpine trade verses, and on the chorus their voices intermingle, sliding between unison and close harmony so you can't always tell where one ends. For a musician whose style grew out of stacking his own voice into dense, genre-blending harmony, this is a close, intimate setting: two singers, one memory.

John Mayer's guitar threads through it. His electric holds long, clean, sustained notes, more a third voice than a lead. Collier called having Mayer lend his tones a surreal thrill, coming from someone who grew up listening to Mayer's music closely. The trio first played it together in October 2022 at McAlpine's Troubadour show, and the track later found a home on Djesse Vol. 4.

The last lines circle back to the sunlight and the carpet and stop at "held you for a moment," with June left off, the memory cut short before it can finish. The song teaches you how loneliness can disguise itself as company, and lets you feel how tender and how sad that disguise is at the same time.
